description: 22 questions about the BEIR paper, labelled with the PDF pages that answer them. Mixes factual lookups, keyword-heavy questions (exact names and numbers, where BM25 should help) and paraphrased questions that share little vocabulary with the text (where dense retrieval should help).

source.title: BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
source.authors: Nandan Thakur, Nils Reimers, Andreas Rücklé, Abhishek Srivastava, Iryna Gurevych

questions.question: How many datasets and how many retrieval tasks does BEIR include?
questions.ground_truth: BEIR includes 18 English zero-shot evaluation datasets drawn from 9 heterogeneous retrieval tasks.

questions.question: Which retrieval architecture achieved the best zero-shot performance on BEIR?
questions.ground_truth: The re-ranking model BM25+CE (a cross-encoder re-ranking BM25 results) performed best, outperforming BM25 on 16 of 18 datasets and improving on it by about 11% on average.

questions.question: What k and b parameters were used for Anserini BM25?
questions.ground_truth: The default Lucene parameters, k=0.9 and b=0.4.

questions.question: Which single evaluation metric does BEIR report for every dataset, and at what cutoff?
questions.ground_truth: nDCG@10, computed with the Python interface of the official TREC evaluation tool.

questions.question: Why did the authors decide against precision, recall, MRR or MAP as the main way to compare systems?
questions.ground_truth: Precision and recall are rank-unaware, and binary rank-aware metrics like MRR and MAP cannot evaluate tasks with graded relevance judgements; nDCG@k handles both binary and graded relevance.

questions.question: How many first-stage results does BM25+CE re-rank, and which cross-encoder does it use?
questions.ground_truth: It re-ranks the top-100 BM25 (Anserini) hits with a 6-layer, 384-hidden MiniLM cross-encoder trained on MS MARCO with knowledge distillation from a BERT-base, BERT-large and ALBERT-large teacher ensemble.

questions.question: How slow is BM25+CE per query on 1 million DBPedia documents?
questions.ground_truth: About 450 ms on a GPU and 6100 ms on a CPU, the slowest of the evaluated models.

questions.question: How much storage does a ColBERT index need compared with BM25?
questions.ground_truth: ColBERT needs about 20GB for 1M DBPedia documents versus 0.4GB for BM25, and about 900GB for the 15M-document BioASQ corpus versus 18GB for BM25.

questions.question: Why can a keyword-based search engine miss relevant documents that use different wording from the query?
questions.ground_truth: Lexical approaches like BM25 suffer from the lexical gap: they only retrieve documents containing the query's keywords, and they treat text as a bag of words that ignores word order.

questions.question: What does Hole@10 measure, and what values did BM25 and TAS-B get?
questions.ground_truth: Hole@10 is the share of a system's top-10 hits that annotators never judged. BM25 had 6.4% and TAS-B 31.8% on TREC-COVID.

questions.question: After the missing relevance judgements were annotated, how did ANCE's TREC-COVID score change?
questions.ground_truth: ANCE's nDCG@10 rose from 0.654 to 0.735, 6.7 points above BM25.

questions.question: Which BEIR dataset has the longest queries?
questions.ground_truth: ArguAna, with an average query length of about 193 words; all other datasets have short queries of a sentence or a few keywords.

questions.question: What nDCG@10 did BM25 and BM25+CE get on SciFact?
questions.ground_truth: BM25 scored 0.665 and BM25+CE scored 0.688 on SciFact.

questions.question: Why do some dense retrievers favour short documents while others favour long ones?
questions.ground_truth: It comes from the similarity function used in training: cosine similarity uses unit-length vectors with no notion of text length and prefers shorter documents (as TAS-B does), while dot product gives longer documents larger vector magnitudes and higher scores (as ANCE does).

questions.question: How does docT5query expand a document?
questions.ground_truth: A T5-base model trained on MS MARCO generates 40 synthetic queries per document, which are appended to the document before indexing it with BM25.

questions.question: What negatives was DPR trained with, and on which datasets was the Multi model trained?
questions.ground_truth: DPR uses a single BM25 hard negative plus in-batch negatives; the Multi-DPR model was trained on NQ, TriviaQA, WebQuestions and CuratedTREC.

questions.question: Does doing well on MS MARCO tell you a model will do well on unseen domains?
questions.ground_truth: No. In-domain performance does not predict out-of-domain generalization: BM25 trails neural models by 7-18 points on MS MARCO but is a strong zero-shot baseline that beats many of them on BEIR.

questions.question: How did the authors quantify how similar the domains of two datasets are?
questions.ground_truth: With a pairwise weighted Jaccard similarity over unigram word overlap: the sum over words of the minimum normalized frequency divided by the sum of the maximum normalized frequency.

questions.question: What is capped recall and why is it needed?
questions.ground_truth: R_cap@k divides the relevant documents retrieved in the top k by min(k, number of relevant documents) instead of the total, because with more than k relevant documents ordinary recall@k cannot reach 1 and becomes unintuitive.

questions.question: What limitations of the benchmark do the authors acknowledge?
questions.ground_truth: It is English-only, lacks long-document retrieval, covers only pure textual search without signals like recency or clicks, uses at most one or two fields per document, and favours general models over task-specific ones.

questions.question: On which datasets did the cross-encoder re-ranker fail to beat BM25?
questions.ground_truth: ArguAna and Touché-2020, two tasks very different from its MS MARCO training data.

questions.question: What hardware was used to measure retrieval latency?
questions.ground_truth: An 8-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8168 CPU at 2.70GHz and a single Nvidia Tesla V100 GPU with CUDA 11.0.
